title: Advance Medical Directives in India: How to Make a Living Will That a Hospital Will Honour
seo_title: Living Wills in India: Valid Advance Directives
meta_description: How an Advance Medical Directive works in India after the Supreme Court's 2023 order, covering attestation and how a hospital must act on it.
intro: An Advance Medical Directive, commonly called a living will, lets a person in India record in advance that they do not want aggressive life-sustaining treatment if they later become terminally ill or permanently unconscious and cannot speak for themselves. It has been legally recognised since 2018, and the Supreme Court made the execution process considerably simpler in a January 2023 order, which is the procedure that governs it today.

Many people who draft one, or whose family discusses drafting one for an elderly or seriously ill relative, still work from the older, more cumbersome 2018 version of the process, involving a magistrate and a lengthy chain of custody for the document. That version has been superseded. Knowing the current procedure matters because a hospital asked to act on a living will during a medical crisis will look for specific formalities, and a document that does not meet them risks being treated as unenforceable guidance rather than a binding directive.

sections.heading: Where the right to a living will comes from
paragraphs: The Supreme Court first recognised a right to execute an Advance Medical Directive in Common Cause (A Regd. Society) v. Union of India, decided in 2018, holding that the right to die with dignity is part of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution and that passive euthanasia, meaning the withdrawal of life support in defined circumstances, is lawful when carried out through a structured procedure. The judgment set out detailed guidelines for executing, storing and acting on such a directive, intended to operate until Parliament enacted legislation on the subject, which has not yet happened.

The 2018 guidelines proved difficult to use in practice. They required execution before a Judicial Magistrate First Class, who had to countersign the document and forward copies to several custodians, and they built in multiple layers of medical board review before a hospital could act. Doctors and palliative care practitioners flagged that the process was so cumbersome that almost no one who executed a directive could realistically expect it to be acted on in time during an actual medical crisis.

sections.heading: The 2023 order and what it changed
paragraphs: On 24 January 2023, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court, acting on an application from the Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine, modified the 2018 guidelines to make the directive easier to execute and to act on. The order is reported as 2023 SCC OnLine SC 99. The most significant change removed the Judicial Magistrate from the execution process altogether. A directive can now be attested before a notary or a gazetted officer instead, who must ascertain that it was executed voluntarily and record that satisfaction on the document.

The document still needs two attesting witnesses, preferably independent of the person executing it, who sign in that person's presence along with the notary or gazetted officer. The 2023 order also streamlined how a hospital acts on a directive once a patient's condition requires it, replacing some of the more layered review steps from 2018 with a more workable two-board structure, discussed below. Commentators tracking the order describe it as a deliberate response to the practical unimplementability of the original scheme rather than a change in the underlying right.

sections.heading: Who can execute one, and what it must say
paragraphs: Any adult of sound mind can execute an Advance Medical Directive, and it can only operate for that person, not as a general instruction given by a family member on someone else's behalf. The document typically names the circumstances in which the person wants treatment withheld or withdrawn, for example where they are in a persistent vegetative state or facing certain death with no prospect of recovery, and it should name a guardian or close relative authorised to make decisions with the medical board if the person cannot communicate at the relevant time.

There is no single government-prescribed form, and the 2023 order did not introduce one, so most directives are drafted individually or using a template from a legal or medical body such as the organisation that brought the clarification application. What matters for enforceability is less the exact wording and more that the formalities, sound mind, voluntary execution, two witnesses, and attestation before a notary or gazetted officer, are all satisfied and documented on the face of the directive itself.

sections.heading: How a hospital is supposed to act on it
paragraphs: When a patient who has executed a directive is admitted in a condition the directive addresses, the treating hospital is expected to constitute a primary medical board, consisting of the treating physician and other specialists concerned with the patient's condition, to certify whether withdrawing or withholding treatment is consistent with the directive and the patient's medical state. If the primary board agrees, the hospital must then inform the jurisdictional authority so that a secondary medical board can be constituted, independent of the first, to review and confirm the primary board's decision before treatment is withdrawn.

The 2023 order simplified this second layer by removing some of the earlier referral steps to the Judicial Magistrate and collector's office that the 2018 guidelines required at this stage, so the process now runs substantially within the hospital and the medical boards rather than through a court or magistrate's involvement at every step. A family member who disagrees with a decision taken under this process, or a hospital unwilling to act on a directive it doubts the validity of, can still approach the jurisdictional High Court, which retains supervisory authority over the process.

sections.heading: Practical points for drafting and keeping the document usable
paragraphs: A directive that sits in a locked drawer or a bank locker the family cannot access quickly is of limited use in an emergency, so the person executing it should tell their named guardian, close family and usually their regular physician that it exists and where a copy is kept, rather than treating it as a private document to be produced only after the fact. Keeping a copy with the family physician, who can flag it to a hospital at the point of admission, is a practical safeguard the courts' guidelines assume will happen even though no specific registry is mandated by the 2023 order.

It can be revoked or modified at any time by the person who made it, by executing a fresh document following the same formalities, and the most recent validly executed version is the one that governs. Because the directive only takes effect in narrowly defined medical circumstances and never authorises euthanasia by active intervention, families sometimes confuse its scope with broader end-of-life wishes; the document should be read strictly for what it actually authorises, which is withdrawal or withholding of specific treatment in the situations it names, not a general instruction about care.

faqs.q: Do I still need a magistrate to make a living will valid in India?
faqs.a: No. The Supreme Court's January 2023 order removed the requirement for execution before a Judicial Magistrate First Class. A directive is now validly executed when attested before a notary or a gazetted officer, in the presence of two witnesses, after the officer confirms it was made voluntarily.

faqs.q: Is a living will the same as consenting to euthanasia?
faqs.a: No. It authorises withdrawal or withholding of specific life-sustaining treatment in defined medical circumstances, such as a persistent vegetative state with no prospect of recovery. It does not authorise any active step to end a person's life, which remains unlawful in India.

faqs.q: Can a hospital refuse to act on a living will?
faqs.a: A hospital must route the decision through a primary and then a secondary medical board under the Supreme Court's guidelines before acting. If a hospital or a family member disputes the directive's validity or application, the matter can be taken to the jurisdictional High Court, which retains supervisory authority.

faqs.q: Who can execute an Advance Medical Directive in India?
faqs.a: Any adult of sound mind can execute one for themselves. It cannot be made by a family member on behalf of someone else, and it only takes legal effect for the person who executed it, applied to their own future medical circumstances.

faqs.q: Can an Advance Medical Directive be cancelled later?
faqs.a: Yes. The person who made it can revoke or replace it at any time by executing a fresh directive following the same formalities. Where more than one version exists, the most recently and validly executed document is the one that governs.

verification_notes: AUDIENCE: HNI and family-business individuals doing estate and end-of-life planning; domestic readers generally. TARGET QUERY: 'how to make a living will in India' / 'is advance medical directive legal in India' / 'living will attestation notary or magistrate'. DEMAND EVIDENCE: none seen from an analytics tool; inferred from continuing 2023 to 2026 press and practitioner coverage of the living-will procedure, including a 2026 news report still explaining the concept to the public, indicating the topic remains searched well after the original 2018 judgment. That the 2018 judgment in Common Cause recognised the right to execute an Advance Medical Directive under Article 21 and set out the original execution and medical-board procedure is confirmed from two independent sources (SCC Observer case background page and the Vidhi Legal Policy ready reckoner). The 24 January 2023 order, its citation as 2023 SCC OnLine SC 99, and that it was passed on an application by the Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine, are confirmed from two independent sources, the LiveLaw-hosted copy of the order and the official Supreme Court order PDF (main.sci.gov.in), both showing the same date and case numbering (Miscellaneous Application No. 1699 of 2019 in Writ Petition (Civil) No. 215 of 2005). That the 2023 order replaced Judicial Magistrate attestation with attestation before a notary or gazetted officer, retaining two witnesses, is confirmed from two independent sources (the Vidhi Legal Policy ready reckoner and the AZB Partners client note of April 2023). That the 2023 order restructured the primary and secondary medical board process and removed some magistrate and collector referral steps used in 2018 is stated in general terms only, drawn from two sources in agreement on the direction of the change (Vidhi ready reckoner and a secondary legal-news summary), because specific board composition details such as the number of years of specialist experience required varied in how clearly different sources stated them and are therefore left out rather than stated as a precise figure. The (2018) 5 SCC 1 citation for the original judgment is widely reported and used here as the standard citation; the exact page citation of the 2023 order within the Supreme Court Reports was not independently cross-checked beyond the SCC OnLine citation and is therefore not additionally stated.
